<reason>Side A built the stronger path to victory by framing the choice as between guaranteeing biological deprivation (early starts) versus permitting adequate sleep (8:30 floor), successfully neutralizing the "arbitrary line" critique by clarifying the floor allows later starts where needed, and effectively countering the bedtime-shift argument by noting early starts make sleep impossible regardless of behavior. While Side B raised strong concerns about uncertain sleep gains and regressive costs, Side A's biological imperative case, combined with the proposition's explicit acceptance of logistical tradeoffs, provided the cleaner route to victory. Side A's clipped closing was a minor execution cost but did not erase the advantage built in earlier rounds.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's Rebuttal 2 (A4.1-A4.3) effectively answered Side B's pressure questions by conceding the rural commute limitation while showing the 8:30 floor still gains an hour of potential sleep compared to 7:30, and by reframing the funding question to highlight that society already pays for sleep deprivation through healthcare and crash costs, thereby shifting the burden back to Side B to justify why uncertain gains don't justify the mandate.</best_rebuttal>
